summary: Treat hit stop as more than a freeze: shake the victim (not the hitbox) more than the attacker, scale the stop by strength and a per-move multiplier, and blend poses during it, because these small touches stack into hits that feel strong.
takeaways: Shake the victim more than the attacker during hit stop
Shake the model only; never move the hitbox
Shake horizontally on ground, all directions in air, decaying
Scale hit stop by damage times a per-move multiplier
Blend into damage poses over about four frames

principles.principle: Shake the victim more than the attacker, but never the hitbox
principles.why: A pure stop works, but Sakurai always adds shake to sell the hit. If the hitbox shakes with the model, attacks that should connect end up missing.
principles.how: During hit stop, offset only the rendered model: bigger amplitude on the victim, smaller on the attacker, horizontal-only on the ground (vertical shake makes legs clip the floor) and all directions in the air, decaying from big to small over the calculated duration.
principles.anti_pattern: Moving the collision hitbox with the shake, or shaking grounded 3D characters vertically.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate hit stop
principles.quote: As a general rule, hit stop in Smash Bros. is never just a stop— there's always a bit of "shake," too.

principles.principle: Scale hit stop by attack strength and a per-move multiplier
principles.why: Stronger attacks should feel stronger, and a multiplier on top lets a sweet spot feel heavier than its damage and lets guest characters match their original games.
principles.how: Compute hit stop from damage, then multiply by a per-move or per-character factor; for example, give a sword tip a higher multiplier than its base. Lengthen it for lightning and reduce it in multiplayer.
principles.example: Marth's Smash Attack (weak base, strong tip); Ryu's hit stops bigger and Kazuya's smaller at equal damage
principles.quote: This isn't just a difference in attack values, but also the multiplier taking effect— making each hit feel even stronger than the damage dealt.

principles.principle: Blend into damage poses and keep the attacker creeping during hit stop
principles.why: A victim who freezes or snaps into one pose looks stiff; blending over about four frames gives a fluid, satisfying result. A barely moving attacker makes swords look like they're actually cutting.
principles.how: Interpolate the victim into the damage pose across about four frames of hit stop. Advance the attacker's animation so slowly it doesn't move every frame, then resume normally, with a per-attack toggle.
principles.anti_pattern: Freezing the victim in place or snapping straight to the damage pose.
principles.example: A sword fighter's strong swing in Smash Bros. Ultimate: the tip keeps inching upward during hit stop
principles.quote: the motion is smoothly blended across four or so frames, giving a fluid, satisfying result.

principles.principle: Scale shake amplitude with camera distance
principles.why: So the impact looks and feels the same whether the viewer is near or far.
principles.how: When the camera is pulled back, make characters shake comparatively more than usual.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate camera-distance shake
principles.quote: When the camera is pulled back, characters will shake comparatively more than usual.

summary: Leave players a little room to "cheat the system" within your game's rules, because getting gains without losses is fun and memorable, and just following the path you laid out isn't.
takeaways: Strategy means minimizing losses and maximizing gains
Exploits giving gains without losses can be memorable fun
Don't stamp out every balance-breaking trick during debugging
Keep cheating within the game; never parameter rewriting

principles.principle: Leave some within-the-rules exploits for players to discover
principles.why: Getting gains without losses is fun and memorable, and players will try to cheat the system anyway; just following the path laid out for them isn't very fun.
principles.how: When testing turns up a balance-breaking trick that stays inside the rules (luring enemies off ledges, farming a rare high-value enemy, resetting for a result), consider keeping it instead of patching it out.
principles.anti_pattern: Removing every exploit during debugging by reflex, or letting players rewrite game parameters.
principles.example: Dark Souls enemies tricked into falling to their deaths; Dragon Quest metal slime farming
principles.quote: it's okay to let players cheat the system just a bit within the bounds of your game.

principles.principle: Analyze strategy as minimizing losses and maximizing gains
principles.why: Defined this way, strategy applies to every genre with push and pull, and it includes taking a larger loss for an even greater gain.
principles.how: For each system, list the ways players can cut losses, raise gains, and trade a big loss for a bigger gain; make sure meaningful trades exist.
principles.example: Action, FPS, fighting, RPG, RTS, puzzle and gambling games
principles.quote: strategy is how players minimize losses and maximize gains.

summary: Change the character's pose the instant the attack button is pressed so players know their input registered, and size each windup by weighing responsiveness against impact and online lag.
takeaways: Change pose instantly on button press to confirm input
Skip interpolating from idle into the windup
Some attacks need no lead-in at all
Big windups add impact and cover online lag

principles.principle: Snap to the lead-in pose the instant the button is pressed
principles.why: In Smash, responsiveness comes first. Lag from networks or TVs can't be fully removed, but players can be told immediately that their input was received.
principles.how: Skip interpolation from the standby pose: on the first frame after input, show a drastically different lead-in pose. For charge attacks, hold that pose and shake in place.
principles.anti_pattern: Interpolating smoothly from standby to avoid an animation skip, which delays visible feedback.
principles.example: Charging a Smash Attack in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
principles.quote: There's no way to completely eliminate lag from network or TV problems, but we can let players know right away that their input was received.

principles.principle: Size each windup for impact and lag cover, not just speed
principles.why: A game doesn't need lead-ins to work, and instant attacks feel responsive, but a big windup gives visual impact and helps hide network lag online.
principles.how: Give light, spammable moves no lead-in (the hit comes one frame after input) and heavy moves a big, readable windup, always judging the input response.
principles.anti_pattern: Making every attack as quick as possible.
principles.example: Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack (out one frame after input); Final Fight's instant jab
principles.quote: So just making them as quick as possible isn't always going to be the best solution.

summary: Know what each role on a game team does and who covers it, and share the project's objectives with all of them, because the roles only produce a game when they work in tandem.
takeaways: One director usually makes almost all final decisions
Planners turn the director's ideas into spec sheets
Animation needs exaggeration and posing, not just realism
Bug reports need repro steps; managers route them
Share objectives with everyone so roles work together

principles.principle: Share objectives and goals with every role on the team
principles.why: Directors, planners, programmers, artists, sound, UI, tech ops, managers and testers must work in tandem, and nothing gets done without mutual understanding.
principles.how: Organize subteams (e.g. characters, stages) that mix professions, keep the director involved in each, and make the project's goals visible to everyone, not only to leads.
principles.example: The Smash Bros. Ultimate fighter team: planners, programmers, modelers, artists, animators, effect and sound designers
principles.quote: Objectives and goals should be shared with everyone, so the entire team can move forward together.

principles.principle: Have planners turn the director's ideas into programmable spec sheets
principles.why: Spec sheets carry the detailed information about how the game should be programmed; planners also balance gameplay, manage teams and supervise testing.
principles.how: Assign a planner role that writes design documents from the director's ideas and distributes them, and have programmers implement from those documents.
principles.quote: In short, they turn the director's ideas into design documents and distribute them to the team.

principles.principle: Require reproduction steps in bug reports and route each to an owner
principles.why: Bug testers' reports only get fixed when the right team takes them over; play testers' feedback is examined by planning.
principles.how: Have bug testers write how to reproduce each bug, have a manager assign it to the team that owns it, and choose play testers for competitive games with enough skill and perseverance.
principles.quote: After they write up a bug report explaining how to reproduce a bug, a manager assigns it to the appropriate team, who takes over until the bug is fixed.

summary: Make the controls fit the gameplay: one button can carry tapping, timing, reaction and hold-and-release games, so add an input only when it improves how the game feels.
takeaways: One button supports tapping, timing, reaction and alternating play
Rapid tapping is tiring and has fallen out of fashion
Reaction games allow push and pull through fake-outs
Hold-only designs struggle to find game essence
Judge each added control by how it feels

principles.principle: Match controls to gameplay; don't add inputs just because you can
principles.why: A single button can already do a great deal, each addition changes how the game feels, and the simplest approach often plays best.
principles.how: Prototype the core action on one button using a tap, timing, reaction or hold/release pattern, and add another input only if it makes the game feel better.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding control features just because you can.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure and Kirby Super Star one-button minigames
principles.quote: Don't add more features just because you can— instead, consider how each addition will feel to the player.

principles.principle: Build one-button play on timing, reaction, or hold-and-release decisions
principles.why: Rapid tapping is tiring and favors naturally fast tappers, and plain holding has little game essence; deciding when to press, release or let go creates the skill.
principles.how: Ask players to press or release at the right moment (release when the crane lines up), or to alternate (hold to catch eggs, release to avoid bombs).
principles.anti_pattern: Mash-only or hold-only mechanics.
principles.example: Crane Fever, Megaton Punch, Egg Catcher
principles.quote: These games revolve around knowing when to keep the button pressed and when to release.

principles.principle: Let reaction games include bluffing so players can fake each other out
principles.why: Pure reflex tests become push and pull once opponents can feint the signal.
principles.how: In head-to-head reaction games, make the start signal something players can imitate or feint, like making the "kah!" sound with their mouths.
principles.example: Quick Draw and multiplayer Samurai Kirby
principles.quote: These games are a test of reflexes, but they allow for push and pull, since players can fake each other out.

summary: Write your game proposal fast while your motivation is hot, keep it brief and image-backed with only what's needed, and treat showing the game's appeal as your responsibility.
takeaways: Write proposals in one push while motivation is hot
Short sentences, clear topics, images reinforcing the text
Cut graphs, research, plan B and grand vision
Polish, not the proposal, supplies much of the fun
Rejection means you didn't show the appeal well

principles.principle: Write proposals quickly while your motivation is hot
principles.why: Nothing good comes from dragging things out; momentum matters, and the longer a proposal sits, the less fresh it becomes.
principles.how: Prepare first by sorting ideas into main topics and subtopics; once the outline and main points are itemized, go straight into the presentation in one push.
principles.anti_pattern: Droning on, or letting the draft sit.
principles.quote: The longer you let it sit, the less fresh it'll be.

principles.principle: Keep proposals brief, illustrated, and limited to what's needed
principles.why: Keeping things interesting is key, and you wouldn't explain your grand vision to players either; what matters is the right amount of information on each page.
principles.how: Use short sentences and images or photos to reinforce the text; cut graphs, research and the plan B; judge each page's information content rather than the page count.
principles.anti_pattern: Lingering on the grand vision, or assuming fewer pages is better.
principles.quote: Include only what you need, and present it as simply as you can.

principles.principle: Don't expect the proposal to hold all the fun; polish adds it
principles.why: Proposals often lack elements that later become essential; at proposal level Monster Hunter doesn't sound novel.
principles.how: Treat the proposal as the start and plan for polishing to be part of making the game fun.
principles.example: Monster Hunter: hunt monsters, make gear from their materials
principles.quote: In other words, polishing your game is also important to making it fun.

principles.principle: Treat a rejected proposal as your failure to show its appeal
principles.why: The proposal must make funders and talent think "We should definitely do this"; showing the appeal is the presenter's job.
principles.how: When a proposal is turned down, rework how it demonstrates the fun instead of blaming the reviewers.
principles.anti_pattern: Convincing yourself the other party doesn't have taste.
principles.quote: It's your responsibility as the presenter to show off your game's appeal.

summary: If you go independent, keep company management from eating your creative time: Sakurai runs Sora Ltd. as a near-staffless contracting company, directs at partner studios one project at a time, and is paid only from sales to share the publisher's risk.
takeaways: Sora Ltd. exists mainly to simplify contracting with companies
He avoids hiring to stay out of company management
Works on-site as a wandering director, one project at a time
Paid only from sales, sharing the publisher's risk

principles.principle: Keep management overhead from crowding out creative work
principles.why: Creators who go independent and hire a team often get bogged down in the management needed to keep employees paid, leaving no time for the game itself.
principles.how: Before building a studio, weigh the management load; Sakurai instead stays a one-person contracting company, directs on-site at partner studios, and focuses on one project at a time.
principles.anti_pattern: Forming a company and hiring staff by default, then losing creative time to running it.
principles.example: Sora Ltd.
principles.quote: leaving no time to focus on what matters most: creating their game.

principles.principle: Share a publisher's risk by tying your pay to sales
principles.why: The publisher sees no profit until the game is on sale, so taking no fee during development shares that risk with them, though it is a high-risk arrangement.
principles.how: Consider contracts that pay from sales after release instead of a monthly fee, but only if you can absorb earning nothing should the project fall through.
principles.example: Sakurai's Sora Ltd. contracts
principles.quote: I don't ask for compensation during the project as a way of sharing that risk with them.

summary: Check and tune your game's sound on headphones, PC speakers and above all a cheap TV, where most players will hear it, and never sign off on audio from big studio speakers alone.
takeaways: Test sound on headphones, PC speakers, and a cheap TV
Most players hear games through bass-poor TV speakers
Never finalize sound solely on big studio speakers
Avoid changing reference headphones mid-project
Balance environment fixes against your creative vision

principles.principle: Check sound on headphones, PC speakers and a cheap TV
principles.why: TV speakers are the most common setup and lose low frequencies; details tuned only in a pristine studio may be inaudible on everyday speakers.
principles.how: Compare every important sound across several listening environments and fix the problems found in each before approving it.
principles.anti_pattern: Finalizing sound solely on big studio speakers.
principles.quote: More than anything, I recommend not solely using big studio speakers to finalize sound.

principles.principle: Keep a fixed listening reference throughout the project
principles.why: If your listening standard changes, it becomes hard to stay consistent with all the audio you checked before.
principles.how: Use the same reference headphones and speakers from start to finish; delay upgrading them until the project is done.
principles.anti_pattern: Switching reference headphones partway through a project.
principles.quote: If your standard changes, it'll be tough to align with all the audio that you checked previously.

principles.principle: Balance multi-environment fixes against your creative vision
principles.why: Taking the tuning too far can pull you away from the sound you intended, and some outputs matter less (the Switch speakers are already crisp, and many handheld players play muted).
principles.how: Prioritize the environments most players use, and aim for a balance that works across them rather than optimizing for any single speaker.
principles.anti_pattern: Over-tuning for one weak speaker until the creative vision is lost.
principles.example: Nintendo Switch built-in speakers
principles.quote: If you take this sound tuning too far, you might stray from your creative vision, so focus on finding a good balance that works in multiple environments.

principles.principle: When borrowing a sound, match how it sounded on original hardware
principles.why: Mimicking the original game's audio wasn't enough for Ryu; the team wanted to capture how it sounded coming from the arcade cabinet.
principles.how: Reference the source as players heard it on its original hardware, and expect careful trial and error.
principles.example: Ryu's impact sounds in Smash Bros.
principles.quote: we also wanted to capture how it sounded coming from the arcade cabinet— a process that required lots of careful trial and error.

summary: For big titles, give players extensive, well-explained settings and accessibility options (The Last of Us Part I is the model), because today's players arrive with different controllers, needs and experience and should be able to set the game up however they like.
takeaways: Big titles need extensive, user-friendly settings and accessibility
Preview each visual option so its effect is clear
Lock difficulty-lowering assists behind an unlock step
Remap with long-press confirm and visible default buttons
Diverse players need configurable setups, not fixed schemes
games: The Last of Us Part I

principles.principle: Let players configure controls freely, with safe remapping
principles.why: Controllers are no longer simple and players arrive with diverse mindsets and experiences; fixed schemes had value mainly for early, simple Nintendo products.
principles.how: Confirm remaps with a long press so short presses still navigate, show each action's default button, allow named profiles, stick swaps and per-context controls (aiming, swimming, menus).
principles.anti_pattern: A fixed, non-remappable control scheme on modern controllers.
principles.example: The Last of Us Part I control menu; named control settings in Smash Bros.
principles.quote: players are coming into these games with diverse mindsets and experiences, so it's necessary to let them set the game up however they like.

principles.principle: Lock difficulty-lowering assists behind an explicit unlock step
principles.why: The extra step prevents accidental changes, and such assists are acceptable because there's more to the game than fighting your way to the end.
principles.how: Group assists like invisibility, slow motion, grab protection, infinite breath and puzzle skips under a locked menu, and offer presets that set many options at once.
principles.anti_pattern: Difficulty-lowering options that can be switched on by accident.
principles.example: The Last of Us Part I Combat Accessibility and Invisibility Toggle
principles.quote: Requiring this extra "unlock" step is a great way to prevent players from accidentally changing certain options.

principles.principle: Show a live preview of what each setting does
principles.why: The right HUD size depends on personal preference and TV setup, and a preview that clearly shows each option's effect is a quality-of-life feature in itself.
principles.how: Add preview windows for HUD options, graphical aids for HUD and reticle choices, dark and bright scenes on brightness/HDR screens, and let players change these mid-game to compare.
principles.example: The Last of Us Part I HUD size preview and HDR brightness screen
principles.quote: It's great how they have this preview window that clearly shows what each option does.

principles.principle: Add navigation aids and sensory cues for hard-to-read worlds
principles.why: The player sees only a small part of the world, and the more realistic the game, the harder the environment is to read.
principles.how: Offer optional destination arrows, ledge vibration, audio cues near jump or pickup spots, a screen reader for all text, colorblind and high-contrast modes, and motion-sickness options.
principles.example: The Last of Us Part I Navigation and Traversal, High Contrast Display, Screen Reader
principles.quote: the more realistic a game is, the harder it can be to read the environment, so this can really help.

summary: Build explosions in stages (an instant flash, a crisp blast, smoke that takes over, and a natural conclusion) instead of a single burst of fire, and fit each variant to where and how it goes off.
takeaways: Explosions go flash, blast, smoke, then conclusion
Instant flash with rays longer than the blast
Mix black into flashes to read on white backgrounds
Let smoke finish so players see where it happened
Make separate ground and air explosion variants

principles.principle: Stage explosions as flash, blast, smoke, then a natural conclusion
principles.why: Each stage communicates something: the instant flash says something intense happened, the blast is the core of the explosion, and the smoke and conclusion show where it took place.
principles.how: Start with an instant flash whose rays reach past the blast range (mix in black so it reads on white), then a crisp blast with sparks, then black smoke as flames wane, then flickering sparkles.
principles.anti_pattern: Just spitting out a blast of fire and calling it a day.
principles.example: Star Force's five-frame explosion; Smash Bros. explosions
principles.quote: That quick burst of light immediately tells players that something intense just happened.

principles.principle: Keep the hit short but let the explosion visuals finish
principles.why: Clearing smoke instantly would be better for pure gameplay, but a shorter explosion lacks impact and hides where it happened.
principles.how: Keep the damaging hit active for only part of the blast, and let the smoke reach its natural end.
principles.anti_pattern: Cutting explosions short for gameplay convenience.
principles.example: Smash Bros. explosions
principles.quote: Letting the explosion reach its natural conclusion and showing players where it took place is vital.

principles.principle: Make separate ground and air variants of explosions
principles.why: Explosions behave differently depending on where they occur, and each type calls for its own know-how.
principles.how: On the ground, make the blast spread upward and the shockwave follow the floor; add screen flash or shake only when it suits that explosion.
principles.anti_pattern: Using screen shake indiscriminately, since it greatly changes how an explosion feels.
principles.example: Young Link's bombs in Smash Bros.
principles.quote: When it's on the ground, the blast spreads upwards and the shockwave follows the ground surface.

summary: To make something original, don't copy what's fun: deconstruct which part is fun, analyze why (usually risk and reward), and rebuild that element into your own mechanic.
takeaways: Copying fun games won't make yours feel original
Deconstruct, analyze why it's fun, then rebuild
Drifting is fun because it pairs risk and reward
Reward risk after the curve, not during it
Design what's fun as a game, not realism

principles.principle: Deconstruct why something is fun, then rebuild it originally
principles.why: Copying something fun won't feel original; understanding why it's fun lets you rebuild it into a unique work, and practicing the process deepens your understanding.
principles.how: Deconstruct (pick the fun part, e.g. drifting), analyze (why: risk and reward), then rebuild in a new form (e.g. brake to charge, drift, release for a speed burst).
principles.anti_pattern: Copying a fun game wholesale.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's one-button charge drifting
principles.quote: I deconstructed, analyzed, and rebuilt, and that's where I ended up.

principles.principle: Reward risky actions tangibly, after completion, without snowballing
principles.why: A score bonus gives no tangible benefit, permanent power-ups let skilled players run away with it, and some speed is needed so the risk is rewarded.
principles.how: Grant a temporary benefit such as a speed burst once the risky action is done (at the curve's exit), not throughout it.
principles.anti_pattern: Score-only rewards, or permanent power-ups that let skilled players run away with the game.
principles.example: Drifting in Kirby Air Ride
principles.quote: Instead of increasing speed throughout the drift, it's better to increase it after the player clears the curve.

principles.principle: Design for what's fun as a game, not for realism
principles.why: A realistic driving experience leaves little room for creativity; real drifting is slower than grip driving, yet making drifting fun makes the game fun.
principles.how: When realism and fun conflict, side with fun; Sakurai doesn't take cues from his real-world driving hobby.
principles.example: Drifting vs. grip driving
principles.quote: At the end of the day, I design things that I think will be fun as games.

summary: A personal aside: Sakurai buys games digitally because he values the play experience over packaging and space is precious, and the one thing he wants most from digital libraries is a way to sort purchases into folders.
takeaways: Physical copies last; digital is instant and needs no shelf space
Sakurai is Team Digital, valuing experience over packaging
Digital console games cost about the same as physical
He most wants to sort purchases into folders

principles.principle: Let players sort their game libraries into folders
principles.why: For someone who plays lots of games, a way to sort purchases into folders is the thing Sakurai always wants most.
principles.how: In any launcher, storefront or library screen, let users create folders or categories and file their purchases into them.
principles.quote: As someone who plays lots of games, the thing I always want the most is a way to sort my purchases into folders.

summary: Build a game on one analyzed piece of fun, widen the range of play styles instead of rewarding a single perfect line, and when delegated work stalls, rebuild it on clear specs with variety driven by parameters.
takeaways: Built on charge-and-release drifting for risk and reward
Expand play types instead of encouraging perfection
Checklist gave casual players a sense of accomplishment
Rebuilt from scratch in three and a half months
Machines differ through parameters on shared behavior

principles.principle: Broaden play styles instead of rewarding a single perfect method
principles.why: Shaving tenths of a second has game essence, but Sakurai wanted a broader design where players don't converge on one method.
principles.how: Add a mode built for variety, such as a large sandbox with differing power-ups and events, so every session plays differently.
principles.anti_pattern: Designing only around perfection and time-shaving.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's City Trial
principles.quote: Instead of encouraging perfection, a major concept of the game was expanding the possible play types.

principles.principle: Create variety through parameters on one shared behavior
principles.why: All Air Ride machines feel totally different yet share the same underlying behavior, so reworked code let the team change characteristics by tweaking a few numbers.
principles.how: Implement one movement model (plus a few true types, like star vs. bike) and express each vehicle or character as a parameter set that the designer writes and tunes.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride machines
principles.quote: Thanks to our reworked game code, we were able to change characteristics just by tweaking a few numbers.

principles.principle: Give casual players accomplishment through a progressive checklist
principles.why: Sakurai wanted to provide a sense of accomplishment even when players are just casually playing.
principles.how: Build an objective grid where completing one square reveals the clear conditions of the adjacent squares.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's Checklist, before PS3 trophies and Xbox achievements
principles.quote: I did this to provide a sense of accomplishment even when just casually playing the game.

principles.principle: Step in and rebuild on fresh specs when delegated core gameplay stalls
principles.why: After a year of delegated development not a single Warp Star worked right; with new specs and existing assets the game was finished in three and a half months.
principles.how: When core gameplay stalls, have the director return, write new specifications, and rebuild the game logic while reusing finished assets.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving stalled core gameplay delegated indefinitely.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's rebuild at the lead programmer's request
principles.quote: After a year of delegating the development, not even a single Warp Star worked right.

summary: Raise concerns about the game or the team the moment you have them, together with a proposed fix, because only during development can anyone still do something about them.
takeaways: Share concerns the moment you notice them
Developers can fix problems; players can only complain
Bring a proposed solution with every problem
Use an opinion board to surface team views
Listeners should be flexible and decide quickly

principles.principle: Voice concerns immediately to people who can act on them
principles.why: Waiting until after the project only satisfies your ego and upsets teammates; unlike players, developers can still fix things, and quick course-corrections make goals easier to reach.
principles.how: Raise the issue as soon as you notice it and make it visible to the people who can do something about it.
principles.anti_pattern: Hiding your feelings and revealing them after the project ends.
principles.quote: Whether or not your opinion would have changed things, if you wait, it's too late!

principles.principle: Pair every problem you raise with a proposed solution
principles.why: It fosters a constructive dev environment, and your suggestion might end up helping many players; if the team keeps things as they are, hearing their reasons helps you accept it.
principles.how: Present the complaint and at least one possible fix together, then listen to the team's reasons if they decide otherwise.
principles.anti_pattern: Only saying "This isn't good."
principles.quote: Make the problem and the potential solution a set package.

principles.principle: Give the whole team an open opinion board
principles.why: It's important to hear everyone's opinions, and some people won't speak up otherwise.
principles.how: Create a board where any team member can write about how development is going; have the director reply or forward items to the right team.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting posts get lost in the flow without a response.
principles.example: Opinion boards on Sakurai's recent projects
principles.quote: On recent projects of mine, I've set up "opinion boards," where team members are free to write their opinions on how development is going.

principles.principle: Listen flexibly and decide quickly when receiving opinions
principles.why: A broader viewpoint and deeper understanding help you reach solutions quickly, and quick course corrections help the project.
principles.how: Weigh the pros and cons of each opinion promptly and stay open to changing course.
principles.quote: And if you're on the listening end of these opinions, try to be flexible.

summary: Don't lock the camera's center point to the character: let the character move off center, especially vertically, so players can feel their jumps, dodges and drifts.
takeaways: Don't anchor the camera's center point to the character
Reduce vertical tracking so jump height reads
Off-center movement makes dodges and drifts feel impactful
Side-scrollers should show more space ahead
Fit camera framing to gameplay and presentation

principles.principle: Don't track the camera center point fully on the Y axis
principles.why: With the center point anchored to the character, it's really hard to tell how high they jump; letting them rise on screen lets players feel jump height.
principles.how: Zero out or reduce Y-axis tracking during jumps so the character visibly moves up on screen.
principles.anti_pattern: Anchoring the center point to the character's position by default.
principles.example: Super Mario 64 jumping vs. a fighter-tracking camera in Smash Bros. Ultimate
principles.quote: So, the center point shouldn't track on the Y axis— or should at least track less— to let players feel the height of their jumps.

principles.principle: Let the character move off center to sell dodges and drifts
principles.why: Moving away from the center makes dodged bullets and missiles visible, which is much more impactful, and in a drift it makes players really feel the input.
principles.how: Offset the character from the center point in the direction of quick moves, dodges and drifts.
principles.example: Armored Core movement; Kirby Air Ride drifting
principles.quote: This makes it easier to see the bullets and missiles you've dodged, so it's much more impactful.

principles.principle: Frame the camera to fit the gameplay, not just follow the character
principles.why: Good framing improves presentation; side-scrollers want a wider view ahead, while realistic third-person racers may genuinely suit an anchored center point.
principles.how: Choose framing per game: look-ahead for side-scrollers, anchored only where precision racing calls for it.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming the camera should always follow the character.
principles.example: Side-scrollers; third-person racing games
principles.quote: Don't assume the camera should always be following your character, but instead make sure it fits your gameplay and presentation.

summary: Make the pose that freezes during hit stop exaggerated, asymmetric, twisted and clear in silhouette from the game's viewing angle, because it's the most memorable moment of an attack.
takeaways: The hit-stop pose is an attack's most memorable moment
Exaggerate, add twist, avoid symmetrical poses
Start sword hit stop after the blade swings out
Silhouettes must show all four limbs clearly
Check poses from both sides of the screen

principles.principle: Design the hit-stop frame as the attack's key pose
principles.why: Hit stop freezes the instant an attack connects, so that pose tends to be the most memorable, and attack animations affect fun more than any others.
principles.how: Include the moment of contact in animation references and review it on its own; for sword swings, start hit stop once the blade has swung out a bit.
principles.anti_pattern: Starting hit stop before the sword has swung, which loses the "hit" feeling.
principles.example: Smash Bros. hit stop poses
principles.quote: The poses in that moment tend to be the most memorable, so it's important to get them right.

principles.principle: Give every hit pose a distinct silhouette from the gameplay view
principles.why: Smash is viewed from the side, so profile silhouettes matter most, and a minor silhouette tweak can make a huge difference.
principles.how: Make all four limbs clearly visible in profile, and check the pose on both the left and right of the screen.
principles.example: Pyra's pose before and after Sakurai's feedback
principles.quote: One minor tweak to the silhouette can make a huge difference.

principles.principle: Exaggerate, twist and avoid symmetry in attack poses
principles.why: Exaggeration helps movement read from far away, and symmetrical poses or plain sideways bends look far less interesting than a twist.
principles.how: Push poses further than feels natural, break symmetry unless it's deliberately comic, and add torso twist instead of a simple side bend.
principles.anti_pattern: Completely symmetrical poses; simply bending torsos to the side.
principles.quote: As a general rule, you want to exaggerate. This will help your movement read more clearly even from far away.

principles.principle: Keep attacks on the gameplay plane so hits register
principles.why: If attacks stray toward or away from the screen, the hits may not register correctly.
principles.how: Keep attack motion centered in the plane where collision happens rather than angling it toward or away from the camera.
principles.anti_pattern: Attacks that drift toward or away from the screen.
principles.quote: Keep your attacks centered. If they stray toward or away from the screen, the hits may not register correctly.

summary: Make big objects feel big through texture scale, restrained saturation and gloss, matching normal maps and surface detail rather than through shape, because CG objects naturally look like scale models.
takeaways: Big objects usually end up looking too small
Same shape can read huge or toy-like
Enlarge texture loops and painted detail scale
Less saturation and gloss make objects feel real
CG tends to look like a scale model

principles.principle: Fix sense of scale through materials before shape
principles.why: A plastic model shares the real object's shape and color yet looks small; CG naturally looks like a scale model, and shape issues are lower priority.
principles.how: Correct textures, saturation, specularity, normal maps and surface detail first, after the game's atmosphere is established.
principles.anti_pattern: Focusing on the model's shape first.
principles.example: Real object vs. its plastic scale model
principles.quote: Normally, objects made in CG will look more like a scale model, so you have to find ways to make up that difference.

principles.principle: Scale texture loops and detail to the object's real size
principles.why: A texture loop that's too small, or material painted too small, makes a large object look small and fake; normal maps that don't match the asset's scale feel off.
principles.how: Enlarge the repeat and the painted detail (tile spots, grass hue variation), judge it from farther away, and match normal-map detail to the asset's size.
principles.anti_pattern: Too-small texture loops; mismatched normal-map scale.
principles.example: Tile and grass textures
principles.quote: When creating textures like these, a common mistake is not making a big enough loop, or painting the material too small.

principles.principle: Tone down saturation and gloss on large realistic objects
principles.why: Saturated textures are less affected by ambient light and look fake, and too much gloss makes things look like toys.
principles.how: Desaturate realistic assets, limit specular area and strength, add dirt to large mechanical objects, and mix varied hues into monotone plating.
principles.anti_pattern: Overdoing saturation or gloss on objects meant to look real.
principles.quote: Too much gloss will make things look like toys.

summary: If you send players on errands, package them well: fitting rewards, frequent moments of joy, freedom to choose a strategy, a quick trip home, and a hint of mystery tied to your world.
takeaways: Same errand mechanics can be packaged far better
Give useful rewards and frequent moments of joy
Offer route choices: safe and long, or risky shortcut
Whisk players home once the objective is done
Hook errands to a mystery in your world

principles.principle: Package errands with mystery tied to your world
principles.why: Mechanically an errand just sets a few flags, but uninteresting tasks don't motivate; a mystery gives a sense of future developments.
principles.how: Instead of "Go buy me some meat!", send players the same distance to look for a missing girl and investigate a house where strange noises were heard.
principles.anti_pattern: Mundane chores and flavorless back-and-forth fetches.
principles.example: The sick-daughter herb errand vs. the missing-girl rewrite
principles.quote: if you're going to make players move around, there are plenty of better ways to package it.

principles.principle: Give each errand useful rewards and frequent small joys
principles.why: Receiving things that are useful in the game, or watching an enjoyable story unfold, makes the errand worthwhile, and many pleasing moments keep it fulfilling.
principles.how: Place combat drops, foraging finds or an unexpected twist along the route, and make the final reward useful in play.
principles.quote: Within even a single errand, try to include many pleasing moments throughout the experience.

principles.principle: Let players choose between safe and risky routes
principles.why: Players feel better when they choose the path forward themselves.
principles.how: Offer at least a safer, longer route and a more dangerous shortcut to the objective.
principles.quote: They'll feel better if they choose the path forward for themselves.

principles.principle: Skip the trip home once the objective is done
principles.why: As with travel, the journey home isn't as exciting as the journey there; let players focus on the parts that are actually fun.
principles.how: Whisk players back to town automatically, or offer an instant return, after the objective is completed.
principles.anti_pattern: Making players trek back after finishing the task.
principles.quote: I'd say it's better to let players focus on the parts that are actually fun.

summary: To make flight (or speed) feel good, add an opposing force such as falling, crashing or a requirement to fly, because the thrill comes from the risk and from barely scraping by.
takeaways: Flight feels good only when falling is a threat
Add slowdown conditions to make high speed matter
Near-miss risk, like flying under bridges, creates thrill
Open sky with nothing to hit lacks tension
Design each mechanic together with its opposition

principles.principle: Pair every movement mechanic with an opposing force
principles.why: No motion feels complete without an opposing element; risk and reward are two sides of the same coin, like player and enemy attacks.
principles.how: Give flight a falling mechanic, penalty or requirement to fly, and give high speed conditions that slow players down.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding a mechanic without anything that opposes it.
principles.quote: When you're adding a mechanic to your game, think about how to oppose that mechanic, too.

principles.principle: Put obstacles near flight paths so players can thread the needle
principles.why: The great feeling comes from the inherent risk and the sense of barely scraping by; nothing but sky would have no tension.
principles.how: Place ground, water and structures like bridges near flight routes; add terrain or obstacles to space and high-altitude settings.
principles.anti_pattern: Open sky or space with nothing to crash into.
principles.example: Flying under the long bridge in the first Ace Combat
principles.quote: Imagine a game with nothing but sky, with no ground at all to crash into. It wouldn't have any tension.

principles.principle: Tie superhuman movement to interactions with the environment
principles.why: Flight feels good when the interaction with the surroundings is spot-on; hunting for launch spots is fun, and contrast between fliers and non-fliers adds enjoyment.
principles.how: Trigger flight from cliffs and ramps, and include machines or characters that can and can't fly.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride flight spots and machines
principles.quote: I'd say you need to get the player's interaction with the surrounding environment absolutely spot-on.

summary: When a team moves to remote work, survey everyone early and quickly buy what they lack (desks, chairs, reference monitors), because most problems can be fixed with equipment, though productivity will still drop.
takeaways: Survey remote staff early to surface shared problems
Missing desks, chairs and reference monitors were common
A central budget bought equipment fast, skipping approvals
Remote work cut productivity by about 30%

principles.principle: Survey the team early after a big workflow change
principles.why: It was a first attempt and many issues cropped up; the survey revealed problems many people shared (desks, reference monitors, internet, playtesting, social contact).
principles.how: Shortly after switching to remote work, ask everyone what's working and what isn't, then fix the common issues first.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's switch to remote work in April 2020
principles.quote: A little after we started working remotely, I sent out a survey to everyone on the team and asked for their thoughts on how it was going.

principles.principle: Solve remote-work problems fast by buying equipment centrally
principles.why: Many issues could be solved with supplies, a missing desk and chair would cause health problems, and per-company procedures and approvals on a mixed team would eat time.
principles.how: Let anyone send a product link; one budget orders it, ships it to their home, and they keep it.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving each partner company to run its own purchasing and approvals.
principles.example: Sora Ltd.'s supplementary budget for the Smash Bros. Ultimate team
principles.quote: To solve the problem as quickly as possible, I had Sora foot the bill for everyone.

principles.principle: Plan for a productivity drop and stay flexible
principles.why: In Sakurai's estimation, productivity fell by about 30%, and pandemic delays are a real occurrence.
principles.how: Account for reduced output in remote schedules, move rituals like daily test matches online, and look for new ways forward.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC development
principles.quote: But just like with every situation, you need to be as flexible as you can, and ready to find a new way forward.

summary: Don't take the easy way out during development: the hardship fades, but the game and its mistakes last, and every player multiplies the effect of your effort.
takeaways: Hardship fades but the finished game endures
Player count multiplies the impact of your effort
Too many compromises lead to lasting regret
Avoid needless hardship; work efficiently, then serve players

principles.principle: Avoid compromises you'll regret once the game ships
principles.why: You forget the difficulties of a project, but the parts you got wrong stay in the game; Sakurai still remembers a mistake in Kirby's Adventure's ending.
principles.how: When tempted to take the easy way out, weigh the effort against a flaw that will be permanent.
principles.anti_pattern: Taking the easy way out and making too many compromises.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure ending: the screen shakes when it should have flashed white
principles.quote: You'll forget the hardship, but the game will endure!

principles.principle: Weigh your effort against how many players will feel the result
principles.why: If 1,000 people play your game, the impact is 1,000 times your hardship; big audiences sweep the hardship away.
principles.how: Remember that actual people will buy the game, and apply yourself for them.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: over 29 million copies, about Australia's population
principles.quote: If 1,000 people play your game, the resulting impact is 1,000 times greater than your hardship.

principles.principle: Work efficiently first, then do everything you can for customers
principles.why: Sakurai isn't saying workers should go through needless hardship; effort should go into serving players, not into waste.
principles.how: Set up an efficient workflow, then put full effort into what players will experience.
principles.anti_pattern: Needless hardship.
principles.quote: But once we're set up to work efficiently, we should do everything we can to serve our customers.

summary: In spec sheets, write each character-specific tunable value as a plain-language phrase in brackets with a placeholder for the number, so programmers know exactly what to expose and anyone can tune it later without misreading it.
takeaways: Code is the instruction manual; parameters are the numbers
Expose tunable values in a table planners can edit
Bracket plain-language parameters; mark values with O
Keep a separate list of all bracketed parameters
Best for unique specs, not global values

principles.principle: Keep tunable values in an external table, not in code
principles.why: If parameters are hard-coded, every adjustment must go through a programmer, yet parameters keep being tweaked for balance to the very end, after the programmer's job is done.
principles.how: Create a reference table separate from the code that planners can adjust at any time, covering values like walking speed and special-move speeds.
principles.anti_pattern: Writing parameters directly into the game code.
principles.quote: In other words, we create a reference table separate from the code, which the planner can adjust at any point.

principles.principle: Mark parameters in specs with plain-language brackets and a placeholder
principles.why: Specs must state clearly which parts become parameters, and each parameter's meaning must be crystal clear because several people will tune them; terse names leave room for misinterpretation.
principles.how: Write e.g. "Initiate movement at [Special startup X-velocity is O]", rule that anything in brackets becomes a parameter, and keep a list file pairing each phrase with its value. Use it for unique specs, not global values.
principles.anti_pattern: Naming parameters only with terse labels like "X-velocity".
principles.example: "At the same time, decelerate by [Special X-deceleration is O/frame]."
principles.quote: I established a rule that anything inside brackets is turned into a parameter.
